results.summary: This design implements free-running oscillators using combinational loops, with dividers to bring output frequencies below 50 kHz. It is tested by selecting an oscillator via input pins and measuring the frequency on an output pin, while true random numbers appear on another output. External hardware includes a frequency measurement tool. The project aims to verify simulation against real silicon behaviour and also provides a true random number generator.

This design generates a PWM signal with a duty cycle selectable from 12.5% to 100% in 12.5% steps, based on three digital input bits and an enable signal. It is tested by applying logic levels to the inputs and observing the PWM output on an oscilloscope. External hardware includes a signal generator for the 10 MHz clock and an oscilloscope. The project is a configurable PWM generator suitable for educational demonstrations of pulse-width modulation.

This design uses OR gates to drive a seven-segment display to show the letter 'J'. It is tested by flipping switches connected to the inputs to produce the correct pattern on the display. External hardware includes a seven-segment LED display and switches. The project is a simple educational example built in Wokwi.

This design implements Wolfram's Rule 30 cellular automaton in hardware and renders it on a VGA monitor at 640x480 resolution. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor via a Tiny VGA Pmod, setting a 25 MHz clock, and observing the chaotic triangular pattern. External hardware includes a VGA monitor and the Tiny VGA Pmod. The project demonstrates a classic cellular automaton with selectable colour palettes.

This design is an analog buffer formed by two inverters (one large, one small) connected in series, from Matt's analog course. It is tested by applying an analog input on ua[1] and measuring the output on ua[0]. No external hardware is required. The project is an educational analog circuit built at the transistor level.

This design implements a puzzle game where flipping any input switch toggles a corresponding seven-segment segment and its neighbours, with the goal of displaying all digits 0–9. It is tested by connecting microswitches to the inputs and a seven-segment display to the outputs. External hardware includes seven microswitches and a seven-segment LED display. The project is a simple interactive puzzle built in Wokwi.

This design generates an Archimedean spiral (r = theta) on a VGA display. It is tested by setting the clock to 25 MHz and connecting a VGA Pmod; input values control foreground/background colour and rotation speed. External hardware includes a VGA Pmod and optional switches. The project is a visual demo of a spiral pattern generated in hardware.

This design classifies images of digits 0–7 using the 16 most significant pixels of an 8x8 image and displays the result on a seven-segment display. It is tested by setting the 16 feature inputs to represent a digit and observing the output on the display. No external hardware is required. The project is a simple hardware classifier for educational purposes.

This design implements a 4-neuron spiking neural network accelerator using the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model, with weights stored off-chip on an RP2040. It is tested by connecting an RP2040 that streams weights via PIO, or by injecting external spikes for a minimal smoke test. External hardware includes an RP2040 (e.g., Raspberry Pi Pico) for weight storage and streaming. The project is a time-multiplexed SNN accelerator with optional Hebbian learning, designed to fit within a small transistor budget.

This design counts up to 10, one second at a time, and displays the count on a seven-segment display. It is tested by connecting programmable delay lines on the inputs to measure input skew. External hardware includes programmable delay lines. The project is a test design for measuring input skew on the Tiny Tapeout platform.
